name: Caesar
description: Canada's briny brunch guardian: vodka and clam-tomato juice under a celery-salt crown. Sounds alarming, converts skeptics daily.
funFact: Walter Chell invented it in Calgary in 1969, drawing inspiration from spaghetti alle vongole; Canadians now drink hundreds of millions of Caesars a year.

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a highball glass, then roll the outside edge of the rim in celery salt to coat it.
Fill the rimmed glass with fresh ice cubes.
Add the vodka, Worcestershire sauce, and hot sauce, then pour in the Clamato juice.
Stir gently with a bar spoon for a few seconds to combine without disturbing the rim.
Garnish with a crisp celery stalk and a lime wedge, and adjust seasoning to taste.
recipe.garnish: Celery stalk and lime wedge on a celery-salt rim

name: Greyhound
description: A lean, quick two-parter of spirit and grapefruit juice. Tart, refreshing, and faster out of the gate than its bus-terminal pedigree suggests.
funFact: Add a salted rim and it becomes a different dog entirely — the Salty Dog; the Greyhound name is tied to the Post House restaurants at Greyhound bus terminals.

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the vodka (or gin, for a more botanical version).
Top with freshly squeezed grapefruit juice — fresh juice makes all the difference here.
Stir briefly with a bar spoon to combine and chill.
Garnish with a grapefruit wedge if you like and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Grapefruit wedge or wheel (optional)

name: Brandy Alexander
description: Cognac, dark crème de cacao, and cream dusted with nutmeg — a chocolate truffle you can drink. Deceptively gentle for something brandy-based.
funFact: It was John Lennon's drink of choice during his 1970s 'Lost Weekend' in Los Angeles — he reportedly likened it to a milkshake.

steps: Chill a coupe glass in the freezer or by filling it with ice water.
Add the cognac, dark crème de cacao, and heavy cream to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds until well chilled and slightly frothy.
Double strain (through the shaker's strainer and a fine mesh strainer) into the chilled coupe.
Finish with freshly grated nutmeg over the surface.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg

name: Espresso Martini
description: Cold, bittersweet, and crowned with dense crema foam — a nightcap and a wake-up call occupying the same glass. Contains no vermouth and makes no apology.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it at London's Soho Brasserie in 1983 for a customer who asked for something that would wake her up, then mess her up; he first called it the Vodka Espresso.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer while you pull a fresh shot of espresso.
Add the vodka, coffee liqueur, sugar syrup, and hot espresso to a shaker.
Fill with plenty of ice and shake very hard for 15 seconds — the hot espresso needs vigorous shaking to chill and build the crema-like foam.
Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into the chilled martini glass.
Let the foam settle for a moment, then float three coffee beans in the center.
recipe.garnish: Three coffee beans

name: Grasshopper
description: Green crème de menthe, white crème de cacao, and cream shaken into mint-chocolate velvet. A supper-club survivor the color of its namesake insect.
funFact: It is credited to Philibert Guichet of New Orleans' Tujague's restaurant, who reputedly entered it in a 1919 New York cocktail competition and took second place.

steps: Chill a coupe glass in the freezer or with ice water.
Add the green crème de menthe, white crème de cacao, and heavy cream to a shaker.
Fill with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds until the mixture is cold and velvety.
Double strain into the chilled coupe for a silky-smooth texture.
Garnish with a mint leaf or a light dusting of shaved chocolate.
recipe.garnish: Fresh mint leaf or shaved dark chocolate

name: Porto Flip
description: Port, brandy, and a whole egg yolk shaken into custard and dusted with nutmeg. The last commonly cited survivor of the once-mighty flip family.
funFact: Early American flips were heated by plunging a red-hot fireplace poker straight into a tankard of ale, rum, and egg, making the drink hiss and froth.

steps: Add the ruby port, brandy, and egg yolk to a shaker with no ice.
Dry shake (without ice) for 10-15 seconds to emulsify the yolk into the liquid.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds until thoroughly chilled and custardy.
Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into a chilled small wine glass.
Dust the surface with freshly grated nutmeg.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg

name: White Russian
description: Vodka and coffee liqueur smothered in cream — dessert wearing a bathrobe. It ties no room together better than a bowling alley bar.
funFact: It languished in obscurity until 'The Big Lebowski' (1998), whose bathrobe-clad hero The Dude drinks little else for the entire film.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the vodka, then the coffee liqueur, and stir briefly to combine.
Float the heavy cream on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a bar spoon.
Serve as is for the classic layered look, or give it one gentle stir to marble the cream through the drink.
recipe.garnish: None (the cream float is the show)

name: Gin Fizz
description: A gin sour shaken hard and topped with soda, meant to be drunk quickly while the sparkle lasts. Once a standard morning restorative, an idea best left in its century.
funFact: The fizz family entered print in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's bartending guide and became a turn-of-the-century American morning institution.

steps: Chill a highball glass and make sure your soda water is ice cold.
Add the gin, fresh lemon juice, and sugar syrup to a shaker.
Fill with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Strain into the chilled highball glass without ice (or over just a couple of cubes).
Top with chilled soda water and serve immediately — this drink is meant to be enjoyed while it still sparkles.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel (optional — classically served ungarnished)

name: Ramos Gin Fizz
description: Gin, citrus, cream, egg white, and orange flower water shaken into a trembling white column that rises above the rim. As much a feat of endurance as a beverage.
funFact: Demand at Henry Ramos's New Orleans bar was so fierce that he employed a relay of 'shaker boys' — reportedly around 35 during the 1915 Mardi Gras, and they still couldn't keep up.

steps: Add the gin, lemon juice, lime juice, sugar syrup, cream, egg white, and orange flower water to a shaker with no ice.
Dry shake (without ice) for a full 60 seconds to build the foam — this is the workout the drink is famous for.
Add ice and shake hard for another 60-90 seconds until the tin is painfully cold.
Strain into a chilled Collins glass with no ice and let it rest in the fridge for 1-2 minutes so the foam sets.
Slowly pour chilled soda water down the inside edge of the glass until the foam rises into a column above the rim.
Serve immediately with a straw pushed through the center of the head.
recipe.garnish: The towering foam head itself (optionally a drop of orange flower water on top)

name: Bushwacker
description: The Gulf Coast's boozy milkshake apex predator: rum, coffee, chocolate, and coconut whirred into soft-serve with a hidden bite.
funFact: It was born at a St. Thomas beach bar in 1975 and adopted by Pensacola's Sandshaker Lounge in 1980, which turned it into a Florida Panhandle institution.

steps: Add the dark rum, coffee liqueur, dark crème de cacao, coconut cream, and milk (or ice cream) to a blender.
Add the ice and blend on high for 20-30 seconds until completely smooth, with a thick milkshake consistency.
If it is too thin, add a little more ice and pulse; too thick, add a splash of milk.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with grated chocolate or nutmeg and a cherry, and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Grated chocolate or nutmeg and a maraschino cherry

name: Frozen Margarita
description: A Margarita passed through a blizzard until it becomes wearable weather. Salt rim, straw, instant vacation.
funFact: In 1971, Dallas restaurateur Mariano Martinez converted a soft-serve ice-cream machine into the world's first frozen margarita machine — it now sits in the Smithsonian.

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a margarita glass and roll the outside edge in coarse salt, then chill the glass.
Add the tequila, fresh lime juice, and triple sec to a blender.
Add the ice and blend on high for 20-30 seconds until you have a smooth, pourable slush with no ice chunks.
Taste — if it is too tart, blend in a small splash of triple sec or simple syrup.
Pour into the salted glass, garnish with a lime wheel, and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel on a salted rim

name: Miami Vice
description: A frozen odd couple sharing one glass: strawberry daiquiri on one side, piña colada on the other. Crockett and Tubbs in slush form.
funFact: Ordering one means the bar makes you two complete frozen cocktails and pours them side by side; the name nods to the pastel-drenched 1980s TV series.

ingredients.item: Light rum (for the piña colada half)

steps: Blend the piña colada half first: combine 1 oz light rum, the coconut cream, pineapple juice, and 1 cup of ice; blend until smooth and thick, then set aside in the freezer.
Rinse the blender, then blend the strawberry daiquiri half: combine 1 oz light rum, the strawberries, lime juice, and 1 cup of ice; blend until smooth.
Both slushes should be thick enough to hold their shape — add a bit more ice and pulse if either is runny.
Pour the piña colada into one side of a hurricane glass while simultaneously (or alternating in layers) pouring the strawberry daiquiri into the other side, so the two halves stay distinct.
Garnish with a strawberry or pineapple wedge and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Fresh strawberry or pineapple wedge

name: Americano
description: Campari and sweet vermouth stretched with soda — the Negroni's gentler ancestor. Bitter enough to feel adult, light enough to have two.
funFact: It is the very first drink James Bond orders in the very first novel, 'Casino Royale' (1953) — before the Vesper was ever invented.

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the Campari and sweet vermouth.
Top with chilled soda water.
Stir gently once or twice with a bar spoon to combine without killing the bubbles.
Garnish with an orange slice (and a lemon twist if you are feeling classic).
recipe.garnish: Half orange slice, optionally with a lemon twist

name: Bloody Mary
description: A savory meal masquerading as a drink: vodka, tomato juice, and a spice rack's worth of seasoning. The only cocktail routinely garnished with breakfast.
funFact: Fernand Petiot claimed to have first mixed it at Harry's New York Bar in 1920s Paris; when he brought it to New York's St. Regis hotel, it was primly renamed the Red Snapper.

steps: Add the vodka, tomato juice, lemon juice, Worcestershire sauce, and hot sauce to a shaker tin with a few ice cubes.
Roll the drink: pour it gently back and forth between two tins (or two glasses) 4-5 times — this chills and mixes without aerating the tomato juice into froth.
Taste and adjust the seasoning — more hot sauce for heat, more Worcestershire for depth.
Strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Garnish with a celery stalk and a lemon wedge (and whatever breakfast you fancy).
recipe.garnish: Celery stalk and lemon wedge

name: Cape Codder
description: Vodka wading through cranberry juice like a bog farmer at harvest. Tart, rosy, and dressed with a lime wedge for the tourists.
funFact: Cranberry cooperative Ocean Spray first printed the vodka-cranberry recipe in 1945 under the considerably less relaxing name 'Red Devil.'

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the vodka, then top with cranberry juice.
Stir briefly with a bar spoon to combine and chill.
Squeeze the lime wedge over the drink and drop it in.
Serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge, squeezed and dropped in

name: Cuba Libre
description: Rum and cola with a firm squeeze of lime — the lime being the entire legal difference between this and an ordinary rum and Coke.
funFact: Its name — 'Free Cuba' — was the rallying cry of Cuban independence, and the drink spread after Coca-Cola arrived in Havana with American forces following the Spanish-American War.

steps: Fill a chilled highball glass to the top with fresh ice cubes.
Squeeze half a lime (about 0.5 oz) directly into the glass and drop in a spent lime shell if you like.
Pour in the white rum.
Top slowly with cold cola to preserve the fizz.
Give one gentle lift with a bar spoon to combine without flattening the carbonation.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on the rim

name: Dark 'n' Stormy
description: Inky dark rum brooding over spicy ginger beer like a squall over open water. Bermuda's unofficial national drink, with the paperwork to prove its seriousness.
funFact: Gosling Brothers trademarked the name, so in the United States a drink legally sold as a Dark 'n Stormy must be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum.

ingredients.item: Dark rum (Goslings Black Seal for the true article)

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the ginger beer first, leaving about an inch of room at the top.
Float the dark rum slowly over the back of a bar spoon so it sits as a stormy dark layer on top.
Squeeze a lime wedge over the drink if desired and perch it on the rim.
Serve with a straw or stirrer and let the drinker mix the layers.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge

name: El Diablo
description: A devil in a ginger-beer disguise. Blackcurrant liqueur gives tequila a wicked purple grin beneath the fizz.
funFact: It appeared in Trader Vic's 1946 book as the "Mexican El Diablo," making it one of the earliest tequila cocktails in print.

steps: Fill a highball or collins glass with fresh ice.
Add the tequila, crème de cassis, and lime juice directly to the glass.
Stir briefly to combine and chill.
Top with cold ginger beer and give one gentle stir to lift the cassis from the bottom.
Garnish and serve immediately while the fizz is lively.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel and a few fresh blackberries, if you have them

name: Fernet con Coca
description: Argentina's national handshake: brutally bitter Italian amaro tamed by sweet cola. Locals call the foamy pour an art form; newcomers call for water.
funFact: Argentines are so devoted to the combination — affectionately nicknamed the "Fernandito" — that Argentina consumes more than three-quarters of the world's fernet.

ingredients.amount: Cubes, to fill a tall glass generously

steps: Fill a tall glass (Argentines use a cut-down liter bottle or large tumbler) all the way with ice.
Pour in the Fernet-Branca over the ice.
Top with cold cola poured hard from a height — the goal is a thick, proud head of tan foam.
Let the foam settle slightly; do not stir, the aggressive pour does the mixing.
Serve as-is; the classic ratio is roughly 30% fernet to 70% cola, so adjust to taste.
recipe.garnish: None — the foam cap is the garnish

name: Gin and Tonic
description: A crisp colonial artifact of gin, quinine tonic, and lime that turned medicine into an institution. Under UV light, the quinine in the glass glows faintly blue.
funFact: British officers in 19th-century India mixed gin into their daily antimalarial quinine ration to make the bitter medicine palatable.

steps: Chill a highball or copa glass, then fill it completely with large ice cubes.
Pour the gin over the ice.
Tilt the glass and pour the cold tonic water slowly down the side to keep it fizzy.
Squeeze the lime wedge over the top and drop it in.
Give one gentle stir with a bar spoon and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge (or a lime wheel and a botanical like juniper berries in a copa)

name: Gin Rickey
description: The driest of the classic highballs: gin, a whole lime's worth of juice, and soda with no sugar at all. Washington's swamp-summer survival kit, still in service.
funFact: It is named for lobbyist 'Colonel Joe' Rickey, whose original 1880s version at Washington's Shoomaker's bar used bourbon; in 2011 the D.C. Council declared the Rickey the capital's official native cocktail.

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Squeeze the juice of a whole lime into the glass and drop in one of the spent lime halves.
Add the gin.
Top with cold soda water and stir once, gently.
Serve bone-dry — no sugar is the whole point of a Rickey.
recipe.garnish: Spent lime half or a lime wedge

name: Long Island Iced Tea
description: Vodka, gin, rum, tequila, and triple sec conspiring under a splash of cola to impersonate iced tea. Famous for being far stronger than it tastes.
funFact: Despite the name it contains no tea; bartender Robert 'Rosebud' Butt claimed he invented it for a 1972 cocktail contest at Long Island's Oak Beach Inn.

ingredients.amount: 0.5 oz / 15 ml (optional, rounds out the citrus)

steps: Add the vodka, gin, rum, tequila, triple sec, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker with ice.
Shake briskly for about 10 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a tall collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with just a splash of cola — enough for the iced-tea color, not enough to make it sweet soda.
Stir once, garnish, and treat it with the respect its strength deserves.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wedge

name: Mojito
description: Havana's garden in a glass: rum lengthened with soda over bruised mint, lime, and sugar. Beloved by drinkers, quietly dreaded by bartenders in a rush.
funFact: Its supposed ancestor, a rough aguardiente remedy called 'El Draque,' is said to be named after the English privateer Sir Francis Drake.

ingredients.amount: 8-10 leaves, plus a sprig for garnish
Crushed or cubed, to fill glass

steps: Add the mint leaves, sugar, and lime juice to a sturdy highball glass.
Press the mint gently with a muddler just to bruise the leaves and dissolve the sugar — do not shred them, or the drink turns bitter.
Add the rum, then fill the glass with crushed ice.
Stir well with a bar spoon, churning from the bottom to lift the mint through the drink.
Top with soda water, cap with more ice, and slap the mint sprig against your palm before planting it in the top.
Serve with a straw positioned next to the mint so every sip smells like the garden.
recipe.garnish: Generous mint sprig and a lime wheel

name: Moscow Mule
description: Vodka, ginger beer, and lime served in a frosty copper mug that does half the work. Neither from Moscow nor mule-powered, but unstoppable since 1941.
funFact: It was engineered at Hollywood's Cock 'n' Bull pub in 1941 to move two slow sellers at once: Smirnoff vodka and the house-brand ginger beer.

ingredients.amount: Cubes or crushed, to fill mug

steps: Chill a copper mug (or highball glass) in the freezer for a few minutes until frosty.
Fill the mug with ice, then add the vodka and fresh lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir gently once or twice with a bar spoon to combine.
Garnish and serve while the copper is still frosted.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge or wheel; add a mint sprig if you're feeling fancy

name: Paloma
description: Tequila lengthened with grapefruit soda and lime over a salted rim — brighter, thirstier work than its margarita cousin.
funFact: In Mexico the Paloma — 'dove' in Spanish — is widely considered the country's most popular tequila cocktail, outdrinking the margarita on its home turf.

ingredients.amount: For rimming the glass, plus a small pinch in the drink

steps: Rub a lime wedge around half the rim of a highball glass and roll the wet edge in salt.
Fill the glass with fresh ice, taking care not to knock off the salt.
Add the tequila, lime juice, and a tiny pinch of salt.
Top with cold grapefruit soda and stir gently once.
Garnish and drink while it's ice-cold and thirst-quenching.
recipe.garnish: Grapefruit wedge or lime wheel on the salted rim

name: Pimm's Cup
description: An ambulatory English garden: cucumber, mint, and fruit bobbing in gin-based Pimm's and lemonade. Standard-issue equipment at lawn tennis.
funFact: It began in the 1840s as a digestive "house cup" served in tankards at James Pimm's London oyster bar; today tens of thousands of pints pour at Wimbledon every year.

ingredients.amount: 1 sprig, plus a few leaves in the glass

steps: Add the cucumber, citrus slices, strawberry, and a few mint leaves to a tall highball glass or pitcher.
Fill the glass with ice, layering it among the fruit.
Pour in the Pimm's No. 1.
Top with cold lemonade (the British still kind or a lemon-lime soda both work) and stir gently to mingle the fruit.
Crown with a mint sprig and a cucumber ribbon, and serve like it's Wimbledon fortnight.
recipe.garnish: Cucumber ribbon, mint sprig, and a strawberry

name: Ranch Water
description: West Texas hydration protocol: tequila, lime, and aggressively bubbly mineral water. Tastes like dusk on a caliche road.
funFact: Texas lore says ranchers made it by drinking an inch off a bottle of Topo Chico and topping it up with tequila and lime, straight from the bottle.

ingredients.item: Sparkling mineral water (Topo Chico is canonical)

steps: Chill everything first — glass, tequila if you can, and ice-cold mineral water are non-negotiable.
Fill a highball glass with ice and add the tequila and fresh lime juice.
Top with aggressively bubbly sparkling mineral water.
Stir once, gently — the drink should stay spritzy and bone-dry.
Alternatively, drink an inch out of a cold Topo Chico bottle and pour the tequila and lime straight in, West Texas style.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge

name: Screwdriver
description: Vodka and orange juice, full stop. The cocktail equivalent of a firm handshake: simple, direct, and done in seconds.
funFact: Legend credits American oil workers abroad who stirred vodka into orange juice with an actual screwdriver; the name was already appearing in Time magazine by 1949.

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the vodka.
Top with cold orange juice — fresh-squeezed turns this from a mixer drink into an actual cocktail.
Stir well with a bar spoon to fully combine.
Garnish and serve. That's it; that's the drink.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice or wheel

name: Sea Breeze
description: Vodka refreshed with cranberry and grapefruit, tasting exactly like its name suggests. A staple of sunburned patios everywhere.
funFact: An earlier 1920s drink of the same name mixed gin and grenadine — the vodka-cranberry version only took over decades later during the great cranberry-juice marketing boom.

ingredients.amount: Cubes, to fill glass and shaker tin

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice and add the vodka, cranberry juice, and grapefruit juice.
Roll the drink: pour the contents into a shaker tin and back into the glass once or twice to chill and blend without over-diluting.
(No tin? Just stir well in the glass for 10 seconds instead.)
Top the glass back up with ice if needed.
Garnish and serve on the nearest sunny patio.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge or a grapefruit slice

name: Seven and Seven
description: Blended whiskey and lemon-lime soda in permanent disco formation. Two ingredients, one number, zero pretension.
funFact: Tony Manero orders 7&7s at the disco in Saturday Night Fever (1977), sealing the drink's status as official fuel of the polyester era.

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh ice cubes.
Pour the blended whiskey over the ice.
Top with cold lemon-lime soda, pouring down the side of the glass to keep the fizz.
Stir once, gently.
Garnish if you must; the classic is served without pretension.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wedge (optional)

name: Tequila Sunrise
description: Tequila and orange juice with grenadine sinking into a layered dawn. More sunrise aesthetics than mixological rigor, and perfectly content with that.
funFact: The modern version was created at the Trident bar in Sausalito in the early 1970s and went global after Mick Jagger discovered it at a 1972 Rolling Stones tour party.

steps: Fill a highball glass to the top with fresh ice cubes.
Pour in the tequila, then the orange juice, and stir briefly to combine and chill.
Slowly pour the grenadine over the back of a bar spoon so it sinks to the bottom of the glass, creating the sunrise gradient.
Do not stir after adding the grenadine — serve as-is and let the drinker swirl it themselves.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a cocktail cherry on a pick

name: Tinto de Verano
description: Spain's low-effort summer survival fluid: red wine lengthened with lemon soda over ice. Cheerfully unpretentious and served by the pitcher.
funFact: The name means "summer red wine," and many Spaniards order it over sangria, which they regard as a drink for tourists.

ingredients.item: Red wine (inexpensive Spanish red, e.g. Tempranillo)
Lemon soda (e.g. Fanta Limón or sparkling lemonade)

steps: Fill a highball glass generously with ice cubes — this drink should be very cold.
Pour the chilled red wine over the ice.
Top with an equal measure of chilled lemon soda and give one gentle stir to combine without killing the fizz.
Add a lemon wheel and serve immediately, ideally somewhere sunny.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel

name: Tom Collins
description: Effectively gin lemonade with bubbles, served tall and unhurried. A drink so easygoing it was once the punchline to a national prank.
funFact: In the Great Tom Collins Hoax of 1874, Americans told friends that a man named Tom Collins was slandering them in a nearby bar, sending victims off to hunt a man who did not exist.

steps: Add the gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 10-12 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice cubes.
Top with chilled soda water and give one gentle lift with a bar spoon to mix.
Garnish and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel and a cocktail cherry

name: Whisky Highball
description: Whisky, ice, and soda water — a drink so minimal it becomes a meditation. Japan elevated its construction into near-ceremonial craft.
funFact: In Japan the highball became so beloved that Suntory sells it ready-made in cans at convenience stores nationwide.

steps: Chill a highball glass, then fill it to the brim with large ice cubes and stir the ice briefly; pour off any melt water.
Pour the whisky over the ice and stir well (about 10 rotations) to chill it thoroughly.
Top up the glass slowly with chilled soda water, pouring down the side of the glass to preserve carbonation.
Give one single gentle lift with a bar spoon from the bottom — no more — and serve immediately.
Optionally express a strip of lemon peel over the top before serving.
recipe.garnish: Lemon peel (optional)

name: Hot Toddy
description: Whiskey, honey, lemon, and hot water — equal parts cocktail and folk remedy. Prescribed by grandmothers far more often than by doctors.
funFact: The word 'toddy' likely derives from tari, a fermented palm-sap drink British colonists encountered in India, long before Scotland claimed the hot version.

steps: Preheat a mug by filling it with hot water for a minute, then discard the water.
Add the honey and lemon juice to the warm mug, then pour in a splash of hot water and stir until the honey fully dissolves.
Add the whisky and top with the remaining hot water, stirring to combine.
Garnish with a lemon wheel studded with cloves and a cinnamon stick if you like, and sip while hot.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel studded with cloves; cinnamon stick optional

name: Irish Coffee
description: Hot coffee, Irish whiskey, and sugar drunk through a floating lid of lightly whipped cream. Weather protection disguised as dessert.
funFact: Chef Joe Sheridan invented it in the 1940s to thaw weary transatlantic flying-boat passengers at Foynes; San Francisco's Buena Vista Cafe imported the recipe in 1952 and now serves thousands a day.

ingredients.item: Lightly whipped cream (whipped to soft, pourable ribbons)

steps: Preheat an Irish coffee glass (or sturdy stemmed mug) with hot water, then discard the water.
Add the brown sugar and hot coffee to the glass and stir until the sugar dissolves completely.
Stir in the Irish whiskey.
Lightly whip cold heavy cream until it just thickens but still pours — it should not hold peaks.
Float the cream on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a warm spoon held at the coffee's surface.
Do not stir — drink the hot coffee through the cool cream lid.
recipe.garnish: The floating cream lid itself; a light grating of nutmeg is optional

name: Mint Julep
description: Bourbon poured over a mountain of crushed ice and fresh mint until the silver cup wears a coat of frost. The American South's answer to air conditioning.
funFact: It has been the official drink of the Kentucky Derby since 1938, with nearly 120,000 juleps served at Churchill Downs each Derby weekend.

ingredients.amount: 8-10 leaves, plus a large sprig bouquet for garnish
1 tsp sugar with 2 tsp water (or 0.25 oz / 7 ml simple syrup)
Enough to pack and mound the cup

steps: In a chilled julep cup (or rocks glass), gently press the mint leaves into the sugar and water with a muddler — bruise, don't shred.
Add the bourbon and fill the cup with crushed ice, packing it down.
Stir with a bar spoon until the outside of the cup frosts over, about 20-30 seconds.
Mound more crushed ice into a dome above the rim.
Slap the mint bouquet against your palm to release its aroma, plant it in the ice next to a short straw, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Generous bouquet of fresh mint sprigs, dusted with powdered sugar if you're feeling fancy

name: Sherry Cobbler
description: Sherry, sugar, and fresh fruit heaped over crushed ice — the drink that taught 19th-century America to love ice, straws, and afternoon drinking.
funFact: The most fashionable American drink of the 19th century, it is credited with popularizing the drinking straw — Charles Dickens's 'Martin Chuzzlewit' features a character marveling over one.

steps: Add the sherry, sugar, and orange slices to a shaker and muddle gently to press out the orange oils and juice.
Add ice and shake briefly, about 8 seconds — enough to chill without over-diluting.
Strain into a wine goblet packed with crushed ice.
Cap with more crushed ice and crown with seasonal fruit and a mint sprig.
Serve with a straw — the drink that made straws famous demands one.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal berries, an orange half-wheel, and a mint sprig

name: Benton's Old Fashioned
description: Breakfast and nightcap fused into one specimen. Bacon-fat-washed bourbon meets maple syrup, smelling faintly of a diner griddle in the best possible way.
funFact: Don Lee's 2007 creation at PDT popularized the fat-washing technique and is named for Benton's, the Tennessee smokehouse that supplies the bacon.

steps: To fat-wash the bourbon (do this a day ahead): stir 1.5 oz / 45 ml of warm rendered bacon fat into a 750 ml bottle of bourbon, rest 4 hours at room temperature, freeze overnight, then skim the solid fat and strain through a coffee filter.
Add the fat-washed bourbon, maple syrup, and Angostura bitters to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until well chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a rocks glass over one large ice cube.
Express an orange twist over the surface, then drop it in.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist

name: Bramble
description: A gin sour caught in a berry thicket. Blackberry liqueur bleeds down through crushed ice like juice through a hedgerow after rain.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it in 1984, inspired by childhood memories of picking blackberries on the Isle of Wight.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with crushed ice.
Add the gin, lemon juice, and sugar syrup directly to the glass and churn briefly with a bar spoon to mix and chill.
Cap with a fresh mound of crushed ice.
Slowly drizzle the crème de mûre over the top so it bleeds down through the ice.
Garnish with a fresh blackberry and a lemon wedge, and serve with a short straw.
recipe.garnish: Fresh blackberry and a lemon wedge

name: Breakfast Martini
description: Toast and marmalade dissolved into gin. A spoonful of orange preserves gives this citrusy specimen its charmingly sticky disposition.
funFact: Salvatore Calabrese invented it in 1996 after his wife insisted he actually eat breakfast — he brought the marmalade to work instead.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer or with ice water.
Add the gin and marmalade to a shaker and stir with a bar spoon until the marmalade loosens and dissolves into the gin.
Add the triple sec, lemon juice, and ice, then shake hard for 10-12 seconds.
Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into the chilled martini glass to catch the peel bits.
Garnish with an orange twist — or go full Calabrese with a tiny triangle of toast on the rim.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist (or a small triangle of toast)

name: Chartreuse Swizzle
description: An alpine liqueur gone tropical, swizzled through crushed ice with pineapple and spice. Green, glacial, and quietly potent.
funFact: Marcovaldo Dionysos built the drink for a 2003 Chartreuse competition around a 110-proof liqueur whose full 130-herb recipe is known only to Carthusian monks.

steps: Add the Green Chartreuse, pineapple juice, lime juice, and falernum to a highball glass.
Fill the glass about two-thirds with crushed ice.
Insert a swizzle stick (or bar spoon) and spin it rapidly between your palms while moving it up and down until the outside of the glass frosts.
Top with more crushed ice, mounding it above the rim.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the top, add a mint sprig and straw, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a mint sprig

name: Division Bell
description: A smoky toll from the mezcal belfry. Aperol and maraschino ring bright over the char, announcing last call in the prettiest way possible.
funFact: Phil Ward invented it in 2009 at his agave-obsessed New York bar Mayahuel and named it after the Pink Floyd album The Division Bell.

steps: Chill a coupe glass in the freezer or with ice water.
Add the mezcal, Aperol, maraschino liqueur, and lime juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
Express a grapefruit twist over the surface to spray its oils, then discard the twist.
recipe.garnish: Grapefruit twist, expressed and discarded

name: Eastside
description: A gin sour that took up gardening. Cucumber and mint keep everything cool and shaded, like drinking the far corner of a greenhouse.
funFact: It descends from the Southside, the minted gin sour beloved in Prohibition-era speakeasies — the cooling cucumber is the modern upgrade.

steps: Chill a coupe glass in the freezer or with ice water.
In a shaker, gently muddle the cucumber slices with the simple syrup.
Add the gin, lime juice, mint leaves, and ice, then shake hard for 10-12 seconds.
Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into the chilled coupe to catch the pulp and mint flecks.
Float a thin cucumber slice or a single mint leaf on the surface.
recipe.garnish: Thin cucumber wheel or a single floated mint leaf

name: Final Ward
description: The Last Word's rye-slinging descendant: equal parts, zero compromise. Herbal, sour, and strong enough to end arguments.
funFact: The name is a double pun by creator Phil Ward: his 'final' riff on the classic Last Word, with his own surname smuggled in.

steps: Chill a coupe glass in the freezer or with ice water.
Add the rye, Green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur, and lemon juice — equal parts, no compromise — to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until thoroughly chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
Serve unadorned, or express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
recipe.garnish: None traditionally; lemon twist optional

name: French Martini
description: A silky relic of the '90s 'tini boom, foaming pale pink from a hard shake. Contains no vermouth and only one French passport holder.
funFact: Despite the name it was born in 1980s New York — the only French thing in it is Chambord, a raspberry liqueur from the Loire Valley.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer or fill it with ice water while you build the drink.
Add vodka, Chambord, and pineapple juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake very hard for 12-15 seconds — the pineapple juice needs a vigorous shake to build its signature silky foam.
Fine strain into the chilled martini glass so the pale pink foam settles on top.
Let it rest a few seconds for the foam cap to form before garnishing.
recipe.garnish: Fresh raspberry (or a skewer of three) dropped on the foam

name: Garibaldi
description: Two ingredients standing at attention: bitter red Campari beneath a cloud of 'fluffy' aerated orange juice. Breakfast-adjacent and proudly Italian.
funFact: It is named for unification hero Giuseppe Garibaldi because it marries northern Italy's Campari with the oranges of the south.

ingredients.amount: Enough cubes to fill the glass

steps: Squeeze the orange juice fresh — bottled juice will not fluff properly.
Aerate the juice: blitz it for 15-20 seconds with a milk frother, blender, or by dry-shaking it hard in a shaker to make it 'fluffy'.
Fill a highball glass with ice and pour in the Campari.
Pour the aerated orange juice over the Campari and give one gentle stir to marry them, keeping the foamy cap on top.
Garnish and serve immediately while the foam holds.
recipe.garnish: Fat orange wedge on the rim

name: Gin Basil Smash
description: A garden brawl in a glass. Fistfuls of muddled basil turn gin and lemon a vivid chlorophyll green, smelling like summer and tasting like victory.
funFact: Jörg Meyer invented it at Hamburg's Le Lion in 2008 and initially called it the Gin Pesto; cocktail blogs spread it around the world within a year.

steps: Drop the basil leaves into a shaker and muddle them firmly with the sugar syrup to release the oils and chlorophyll.
Add gin, lemon juice, and plenty of ice.
Shake very hard for 12-15 seconds — the harder the shake, the greener the drink.
Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into a rocks glass filled with fresh ice, leaving the basil shreds behind.
Slap a basil sprig against your palm to wake up its aroma and garnish.
recipe.garnish: Fresh basil sprig

name: Gin-Gin Mule
description: A diplomatic summit between the Mojito and the Moscow Mule, chaired by gin. Ginger beer provides the fireworks; mint signs the accords.
funFact: Audrey Saunders designed it around 2000 as a gateway drink to convert vodka drinkers to gin, and it became her Pegu Club's calling card.

ingredients.amount: 6-8 leaves, plus a sprig for garnish

steps: Gently muddle the mint leaves with the simple syrup in a shaker — press, don't pulverize.
Add gin, lime juice, and ice, then shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Double strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold, spicy ginger beer and give one gentle lift with a barspoon to integrate.
Garnish with a slapped mint sprig and a lime wheel.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and a lime wheel

name: Gold Rush
description: Prospector's treasure in liquid form: bourbon panned through honey and lemon until only the nuggets remain. Simple, gleaming, and dangerously repeatable.
funFact: T.J. Siegal created it at Milk & Honey in 2001 by swapping honey syrup into a whiskey sour, using the honey mix the bar kept for its Bee's Knees.

ingredients.amount: 0.75 oz / 22 ml (3 parts honey : 1 part hot water, cooled)

steps: Make the honey syrup ahead: stir honey with a splash of hot water until pourable, then let it cool.
Add bourbon, honey syrup, and lemon juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until the tin is frosty.
Strain over one large ice cube in a chilled rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the surface if you like a brighter nose, then drop it in or discard.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist (optional — classically served clean)

name: Kentucky Buck
description: A bourbon buck with strawberry stains on its boots. Ginger beer kicks, fruit soothes, and the whole ride tastes like summer in the bluegrass.
funFact: Erick Castro created it at San Francisco's Rickhouse around 2010, and it became one of the most reprinted modern recipes in the ginger-spiked 'buck' family.

steps: Muddle the strawberry with the simple syrup in the bottom of a shaker until fully crushed.
Add bourbon, lemon juice, bitters, and ice, then shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold ginger beer and stir once, gently, from the bottom up.
Garnish with a strawberry slice and a lemon wheel on the rim.
recipe.garnish: Strawberry slice and lemon wheel

name: Naked and Famous
description: A smoky equal-parts hybrid that shows all its cards at once. Mezcal growls, Chartreuse hums, and Aperol keeps the whole confession bright.
funFact: Creator Joaquín Simó of Death & Co described it as the bastard love child of the Last Word and the Paper Plane, born in the mountains of Oaxaca.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Add all four ingredients — equal parts, no exceptions — to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until well chilled and slightly aerated.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
Serve as-is; the drink is traditionally left ungarnished so the smoke and herbs speak for themselves.
recipe.garnish: None (optionally a lime wheel on the rim)

name: Oaxaca Old Fashioned
description: An agave-speaking cousin of the bourbon original. Tequila carries the melody, mezcal supplies the campfire, and a flamed orange twist lights the way.
funFact: Phil Ward's 2007 Death & Co creation is widely credited with helping kick off the American mezcal boom.

steps: Add agave nectar, bitters, mezcal, and tequila to a mixing glass.
Fill with ice and stir for 20-30 seconds until well chilled and slightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Cut a wide swath of orange peel; carefully warm it over a lit match, then pinch it skin-side down over the drink so the oils flame across the surface.
Drop the flamed twist into the glass and serve.
recipe.garnish: Flamed orange twist

name: Old Cuban
description: A Mojito that came into money. Aged rum and mint get dressed up with Champagne, trading the beach for a hotel ballroom.
funFact: Audrey Saunders, who later founded New York's influential Pegu Club, invented it in the early 2000s as a bridge between the Mojito and the French 75.

ingredients.amount: Top with ~2 oz / 60 ml, well chilled

steps: Chill a coupe and make sure the Champagne is ice cold.
Gently muddle the mint leaves with the sugar syrup in a shaker.
Add aged rum, lime juice, Angostura bitters, and ice, then shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Double strain into the chilled coupe to catch every fleck of mint.
Top gently with Champagne and float a pretty mint leaf on the surface.
recipe.garnish: Single mint leaf floated on top

name: Porn Star Martini
description: A flamboyant passion fruit showpiece that arrives with its own entourage: a chilled shot of sparkling wine served on the side, for sipping between scenes.
funFact: Douglas Ankrah created it in 2002, and it has repeatedly ranked as the United Kingdom's most-ordered cocktail.

ingredients.amount: 2 oz / 60 ml, chilled, in a shot glass

steps: Chill a coupe and a shot glass in the freezer.
Add vanilla vodka, passion fruit liqueur, passion fruit purée, and lime juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake very hard for 12-15 seconds to chill and build a golden foam.
Fine strain into the chilled coupe.
Float half a passion fruit cut-side up on the foam, and pour the chilled sparkling wine into the shot glass.
Serve the shot alongside — sip it between tastes or tip it in, dealer's choice.
recipe.garnish: Half a passion fruit floated on the foam; sparkling wine shot on the side

name: Red Hook
description: A Manhattan that moved across the river and got tougher. Punt e Mes brings the bitterness, maraschino whispers dark cherry down by the docks.
funFact: Vincenzo Errico created it at Milk & Honey in 2003, sparking a whole borough of Brooklyn-neighborhood riffs like the Greenpoint and the Bensonhurst.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Add rye, Punt e Mes, and maraschino liqueur to a mixing glass filled with ice.
Stir for 20-30 seconds until well chilled and silky.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Drop in a brandied cherry and serve.
recipe.garnish: Brandied or maraschino cherry

name: Tommy's Margarita
description: A Margarita stripped to its agave soul: no orange liqueur, just tequila, lime, and nectar from the same plant that made the spirit. Purists nod; the plant approves.
funFact: Julio Bermejo created it at his family's Tommy's Mexican Restaurant in San Francisco in the early 1990s, and the IBA later added it to its official cocktail list.

steps: If you like a salt rim, rub a lime wedge around half the rim of a rocks glass and dip it in coarse salt, then fill the glass with fresh ice.
Add tequila, lime juice, and agave nectar to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until frosty.
Strain into the prepared rocks glass over the fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel and serve.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel; optional half salt rim

name: Trinidad Sour
description: A rule-breaker that uses bitters as the base spirit rather than the seasoning. Orgeat and lemon tame a full pour of Angostura into crimson velvet.
funFact: Giuseppe González's 2009 recipe calls for a staggering ounce and a half of Angostura bitters — more than most bars use in a week of dashes.

ingredients.amount: 1.5 oz / 45 ml (yes, really — it is the base)

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Remove the dasher cap from the Angostura bottle so you can free-pour a full measure.
Add the bitters, orgeat, lemon juice, and rye to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds — the orgeat needs a strong shake to emulsify into crimson velvet.
Double strain into the chilled coupe and serve.
recipe.garnish: None traditionally; a lemon twist if you must

name: White Negroni
description: A pale doppelgänger of Italy's famous bitter, rebuilt from French parts. Gentian root supplies the bite while Lillet smooths the edges to ivory.
funFact: British bartender Wayne Collins improvised it at a Bordeaux wine fair in 2001 when he couldn't find Campari and sweet vermouth, so he grabbed Suze and Lillet instead.

steps: Add gin, Lillet Blanc, and Suze to a mixing glass filled with ice.
Stir for 20-30 seconds until thoroughly chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the surface to mist it with citrus oil.
Drop the twist in and serve.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist

name: Dirty Shirley
description: A Shirley Temple that came of age and ordered vodka. Grenadine-sweet nostalgia with a fake ID.
funFact: The New York Times crowned it the 'drink of the summer' in 2022, decades after the mocktail it corrupts was named for child star Shirley Temple.

ingredients.amount: 0.5 oz / 15 ml (real pomegranate grenadine if possible)
2-3 cherries, plus a splash of their syrup if you like it sweeter

steps: Fill a highball glass to the top with ice.
Pour in the vodka, then the grenadine.
Top with cold lemon-lime soda, leaving a little room at the rim.
Give one gentle stir with a barspoon so the grenadine ribbons up without killing the bubbles.
Drop in the maraschino cherries and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Maraschino cherries (skewered or dropped in)

name: Jell-O Shot
description: A wobbling gelatin lifeform that carries liquor in structural form. Consumed by the tray, respected by no one, beloved by all.
funFact: Satirist Tom Lehrer claimed to have pioneered it in the 1950s to sneak liquor onto an Army base where drinks were banned at the Christmas party.

steps: Pour the gelatin powder into a heatproof bowl or measuring jug with a spout.
Add 8 oz / 240 ml just-boiled water and stir for a full 2 minutes until the gelatin is completely dissolved.
Stir in 6 oz / 180 ml chilled vodka and 2 oz / 60 ml cold water.
Pour into ~16 small 2-oz plastic cups, filling each about two-thirds full.
Refrigerate at least 2-4 hours until fully set; keep cold until serving.
recipe.garnish: Optional dollop of whipped cream on each cup

name: Fish House Punch
description: Jamaican rum, cognac, and peach brandy loosened with lemon and sugar in a communal bowl. Colonial America's most storied — and most underestimated — punch.
funFact: It was born in 1732 at Philadelphia's Schuylkill Fishing Company, a colonial angling club, and legend blames a conspicuously blank stretch in George Washington's diary on an encounter with it.

steps: Add the rum, cognac, peach brandy, lemon juice, sugar syrup, and water or cold tea to a mixing glass or small pitcher.
Stir briefly to integrate, then pour over a large ice cube (or one big block if scaling up) in a punch cup or rocks glass.
Stir 10-15 seconds to chill and slightly dilute.
Grate a little fresh nutmeg over the top and add a lemon wheel.
To batch for a bowl, multiply everything by 8-10, stir over a large ice block, and let it mellow 20 minutes before serving.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a lemon wheel

name: Sangria
description: Red wine steeped with chopped fruit, sweetener, and often a shot of brandy, served by the pitcher. Spain's most sociable export after the siesta.
funFact: Named for 'sangre' — Spanish for blood — it conquered the United States at the Spanish Pavilion of the 1964 New York World's Fair.

ingredients.item: Dry Spanish red wine (Tempranillo or Garnacha)

steps: Chop an orange, an apple, and half a lemon into bite-size pieces and add them to a large pitcher.
Pour in the wine, brandy, and simple syrup; add the cinnamon stick if using, and stir well.
Cover and refrigerate 2-4 hours (up to overnight) so the fruit infuses.
Taste and adjust sweetness with a little more syrup if the wine is very dry.
Serve in wine glasses over a few ice cubes, spooning some of the soaked fruit into each glass.
recipe.garnish: Wine-soaked fruit and an orange slice on the rim

name: Batanga
description: Tequila and cola with a salted rim, stirred — by decree of its late inventor — with a well-worn kitchen knife. Humble ingredients, sacred technique.
funFact: Don Javier Delgado Corona invented it in 1961 at La Capilla in the town of Tequila and stirred every Batanga with the same knife he used to cut limes, tending his bar into his nineties.

ingredients.item: Mexican cola (from a glass bottle if possible)

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a highball glass and roll the rim in coarse salt.
Fill the glass with ice, then add the tequila and fresh lime juice.
Top with cola, pouring gently to keep the fizz.
Stir once, tradition says with a kitchen knife, from the bottom up to combine.
Serve with the spent lime wedge dropped in.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on the salted rim

name: Cantarito
description: Tequila and a citrus grove sharing a rustic clay cup. The vessel sweats, the drink stays cool, and Jalisco road trips suddenly make sense.
funFact: It is named for the little porous clay cup it's served in, which chills the drink through evaporation — devotees insist the cup drinks better with years of use.

steps: If you have a clay cantarito cup, soak it in cold water for a few minutes; otherwise use a highball glass, optionally with a salted rim.
Fill the cup with ice and add the tequila, lime, orange, and grapefruit juices with a pinch of salt.
Stir briefly to combine and dissolve the salt.
Top with grapefruit soda and give one gentle stir.
Garnish and serve immediately while the clay is still cool.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel and a grapefruit or orange wedge

name: Carajillo
description: Espresso fortified for active duty. On its Mexican tour it drafts vanilla-citrus Licor 43, foaming over ice into a caffeinated nightcap.
funFact: Folk etymology traces the name to 'coraje' — courage — from Spanish soldiers in colonial Cuba who spiked their coffee before duty.

steps: Pull a fresh double shot of espresso and let it sit while you prepare the glass.
Fill a rocks glass with large ice cubes and pour in the Licor 43.
Slowly pour the hot espresso over the ice so it floats in a dark layer on top.
Serve as is for the layered look, or stir once to integrate; for a frothy top, shake liqueur and espresso hard with ice for 10 seconds and strain over fresh ice instead.
recipe.garnish: 3 coffee beans (optional)

name: Coquito
description: Puerto Rico's coconut Christmas elixir, thick as a lullaby and spiced with cinnamon. Appears in December, vanishes by Three Kings Day.
funFact: The name means "little coconut," and Puerto Rican families guard their recipes so fiercely that coquito tasting contests are a holiday institution.

steps: Add the coconut cream, coconut milk, sweetened condensed milk, rum, and ground cinnamon to a blender.
Blend on high for 1-2 minutes until completely smooth and slightly frothy.
Pour into a bottle or pitcher and refrigerate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, so it thickens and the flavors marry.
Shake the bottle well before serving, since the coconut fat separates as it chills.
Serve in small chilled glasses with a dusting of cinnamon on top.
recipe.garnish: Dusting of ground cinnamon and a cinnamon stick

name: Kalimotxo
description: Equal parts red wine and cola — the Basque Country's shrug at wine snobbery. Somehow far more than the sum of its cheap, brilliant parts.
funFact: As the story goes, it was christened at a 1972 Basque port festival when vendors rescued a batch of off wine by cutting it with Coca-Cola.

steps: Chill both the wine and the cola thoroughly beforehand.
Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in equal parts red wine and cola.
Stir once gently to combine without killing the fizz.
Add a lemon wedge and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wedge

name: Michelada
description: Beer that went to battle and came back seasoned: lime, hot sauce, and a salted rim turn a lager into brunchtime armor.
funFact: One popular origin story credits Michel Ésper, a regular at a San Luis Potosí sports club, whose custom beer-and-lime order became "Michel-ada" — Michel's lemonade.

ingredients.item: Coarse salt or Tajín (for the rim)

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a chilled pint glass and roll the rim in coarse salt or Tajín.
Fill the glass with ice, then add the lime juice, hot sauce, and Worcestershire sauce.
Stir briefly to combine the seasonings.
Slowly pour in the cold lager, tilting the glass to preserve the head.
Serve with the rest of the bottle on the side for topping up as you drink.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on the salted rim

name: Queen's Park Swizzle
description: A Trinidadian tower of crushed ice, demerara rum, and mint, capped by a rust-red stratum of Angostura. Requires a swizzle stick and forearm commitment.
funFact: Born at Port of Spain's Queen's Park Hotel in the 1920s, it was praised by Trader Vic as "the most delightful form of anesthesia given out today."

steps: Gently press the mint leaves with the demerara syrup in the bottom of a highball glass to release their oils, without shredding them.
Add the rum and lime juice, then pack the glass with crushed ice.
Insert a swizzle stick (or barspoon) and spin it briskly between your palms, moving up and down, until the outside of the glass frosts over.
Top with more crushed ice, mounding it slightly above the rim.
Dash the Angostura bitters generously over the ice cap so it forms a red layer, and garnish.
recipe.garnish: Bouquet of slapped mint over the bitters-stained ice cap

name: Sgroppino
description: A Venetian slush of lemon sorbet whipped with prosecco and vodka. Half dessert, half palate cleanser, entirely committed to elegance.
funFact: Its name comes from Venetian dialect for untying a little knot — it was traditionally served between courses to loosen the palate at Venetian banquets.

steps: Chill a champagne flute, a small bowl, and a whisk in the freezer for 10 minutes.
In the cold bowl, whisk the lemon sorbet with the vodka until it loosens into a smooth cream.
Add the prosecco a little at a time, whisking gently after each pour until the mix is velvety and frothy but still pourable.
Pour into the chilled flute.
Garnish and serve immediately with a small spoon, before it separates.
recipe.garnish: Twist of lemon zest or a small mint leaf

name: Terremoto
description: Chile's 'earthquake': sweet young pipeño wine capped with a scoop of pineapple ice cream. The ground feels perfectly stable until you stand up.
funFact: Santiago lore says foreign journalists covering the 1985 earthquake named it for its ground-shifting effects — and a second round is called a réplica, an aftershock.

ingredients.item: Pipeño (or another sweet, young white wine)

steps: Chill a large tumbler or pint glass; no ice is needed, the ice cream does the chilling.
Pour in the cold pipeño, leaving room at the top.
Float a generous scoop of pineapple ice cream on the wine.
Drizzle the grenadine over the ice cream (or substitute a float of fernet for the drier, Santiago-bar version).
Serve with a straw and a long spoon, stirring as little or as much as you dare.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; a pineapple wedge if you like

name: Ti' Punch
description: Martinique's minimalist ritual: grassy rhum agricole, a coin of lime, and a slick of cane syrup. No ice unless you ask, no apologies either way.
funFact: Caribbean custom dictates "chacun prépare sa propre mort" — each prepares his own death — so the bartender hands you the bottle and you mix your own.

ingredients.item: Rhum agricole blanc (100 proof if you can find it)
Lime disc (a coin of peel with a little flesh)

steps: Cut a small coin of lime, mostly peel with a thin edge of flesh, from the side of a lime.
Squeeze the lime disc over a small tumbler and drop it in.
Add the cane syrup and muddle it briefly with the lime coin.
Pour in the rhum agricole and stir a few seconds with a small spoon until the syrup dissolves.
Serve neat at room temperature in the traditional style, or add a single small ice cube if you must.
recipe.garnish: The lime disc in the glass

name: Appletini
description: A neon-green Jolly Rancher of a drink from the height of the 'tini era. Tastes of sour apple candy; contains no measurable apple.
funFact: It debuted at Lola's in West Hollywood in 1997 as the "Adam's Apple Martini," named for the bartender who created it.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Add the vodka, sour apple schnapps, and lemon juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until the tin is frosty.
Empty the martini glass and double-strain the drink into it through a fine mesh strainer.
Garnish and serve straight up.
recipe.garnish: Thin slice of green apple on the rim

name: Fuzzy Navel
description: Peach schnapps and orange juice in unapologetic harmony. Soft, sweet, and named after a pun rather than a body part, honest.
funFact: The name is a double pun — fuzzy for the peach, navel for the orange — and the drink helped make 1980s peach schnapps one of the fastest-selling new liquors in US history.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the peach schnapps.
Top with cold orange juice.
Stir well to combine.
Garnish with an orange slice and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice on the rim

name: Harvey Wallbanger
description: A Screwdriver crowned with a golden float of herbal Galliano. Its groovy name and cartoon mascot did most of the heavy lifting in the 1970s.
funFact: A 1970s Galliano marketing campaign built the drink around a sandal-wearing cartoon surfer whose slogan was "Harvey Wallbanger is the name. And I can be made!"

steps: Fill a highball glass to the top with fresh ice cubes.
Pour the vodka over the ice, then top with the orange juice and give it a brief stir to combine.
Float the Galliano on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a bar spoon so it sits as a golden layer.
Garnish and serve with a straw, letting the drinker stir the float in as they sip.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a maraschino cherry

name: Midori Sour
description: A radioactive-green melon sour beamed straight from a 1980s dance floor. Sweet, kitschy, and completely unashamed of either.
funFact: Midori means 'green' in Japanese, and Suntory launched the liqueur in America with a 1978 party at Studio 54.

steps: Add the Midori, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a cocktail shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until the tin is frosty.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
If you like it lighter and fizzy, top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel and a maraschino cherry (or a honeydew melon ball)

name: Mudslide
description: A milkshake that took a wrong turn into the liquor cabinet. Vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream engulf everything in delicious sediment.
funFact: It was reportedly invented in the 1970s at the Wreck Bar at Rum Point on Grand Cayman, where it remains the house specialty.

steps: Optionally drizzle chocolate syrup around the inside of a chilled hurricane or rocks glass.
Add the vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until well chilled and slightly frothy.
Strain over fresh ice in the prepared glass.
For a frozen version, blend everything with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a cup of ice instead of shaking.
Garnish and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Chocolate syrup drizzle; whipped cream and chocolate shavings optional

name: Rusty Nail
description: Scotch sweetened by Drambuie's honeyed herbs, sipped slowly in leather-chair lighting. The official nightcap of ring-a-ding-ding.
funFact: Drambuie, its defining half, is tied to a legend that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the secret recipe to the MacKinnon clan after the failed 1745 Jacobite rising.

steps: Add the Scotch and Drambuie to a mixing glass filled with ice.
Stir gently for 20-30 seconds until well chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain into a rocks glass over one large ice cube.
Express a lemon twist over the surface, then drop it in or rest it on the rim.
Sip slowly; adjust to equal parts Scotch and Drambuie if you prefer it sweeter.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist

name: B-52
description: A three-layer stratigraphy of coffee liqueur, Irish cream, and orange liqueur. Drink it fast or set the top alight; geology was never this festive.
funFact: A popular origin story credits Alberta bartender Peter Fich, who named his layered creations after favorite bands — this one for the B-52s.

steps: Pour the coffee liqueur into a shot glass as the bottom layer.
Hold a bar spoon upside down just above the surface and slowly pour the Irish cream over its back so it floats in a distinct second layer.
Repeat with the orange liqueur over the spoon to form the clear top layer.
Serve immediately while the three layers are sharp; drink in one go or sip through the strata.
recipe.garnish: None (the three clean layers are the presentation)

name: Baby Guinness
description: A trompe-l'oeil shooter: coffee liqueur topped with a float of Irish cream so it resembles a miniature pint of stout, foam collar and all.
funFact: Despite the name and the perfect two-tone pour, it contains no Guinness at all.

steps: Pour the coffee liqueur into a shot glass, filling it about two-thirds of the way.
Hold a bar spoon upside down just above the liqueur and pour the Irish cream slowly over its back so it settles into a creamy head.
Let it sit a few seconds so the 'foam collar' sharpens into a miniature pint of stout.
Serve immediately and drink in one go.
recipe.garnish: None (the Irish cream head is the garnish)

name: Buttery Nipple
description: A dessert-counter shooter of butterscotch schnapps under a cool cream float. Zero sophistication, one hundred percent compliance.
funFact: The layering is pure physics: sugar-dense butterscotch schnapps sinks while the lighter Irish cream floats serenely on top.

steps: Chill the butterscotch schnapps (fridge or a quick stir over ice, strained) for a smoother shot.
Pour the schnapps into a shot glass, filling it about two-thirds full.
Slowly pour the Irish cream over the back of a bar spoon so it floats on top; the denser schnapps stays below.
Serve immediately and drink in one smooth go.
recipe.garnish: None

name: Green Tea Shot
description: Irish whiskey and peach schnapps masquerading as a health beverage. Named purely for its jade hue — no leaves were steeped in its making.
funFact: It contains no tea whatsoever — the name comes entirely from the drink's pale green color.

ingredients.item: Sour mix (or equal parts lemon juice and simple syrup)

steps: Add the whiskey, peach schnapps, and sour mix to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 8-10 seconds until very cold.
Strain into a chilled shot glass, leaving a little room at the top.
Top with a splash of lemon-lime soda for the signature fizz.
Drink in one go while it's ice cold.
recipe.garnish: None (a thin lemon wedge on the rim is optional)

name: Jägerbomb
description: A depth charge of German herbal liqueur plunged into an energy drink. The splash is part of the ceremony; the regret is complimentary.
glassware: Shot glass dropped in a pint glass
funFact: Jägermeister means "master hunter," and the glowing stag on its label honors St. Hubertus, the patron saint of hunters.

ingredients.item: Jagermeister (well chilled, ideally from the freezer)

steps: Pour the energy drink into a sturdy pint or highball glass, filling it about a third of the way.
Fill a shot glass with the ice-cold Jagermeister.
Drop the full shot glass straight into the glass of energy drink — glass and all.
Drink immediately in one continuous go while it fizzes.
Mind your teeth on the shot glass as you finish.
recipe.garnish: None

name: Kamikaze
description: Vodka, orange liqueur, and lime in equal thirds — a citrus dive-bomb with no survivors expected. Clean, sharp, and gone in one motion.
funFact: Add a splash of cranberry, serve it up in a stemmed glass, and the 1970s Kamikaze becomes the blueprint of the Cosmopolitan.

steps: Add the vodka, triple sec, and lime juice — equal thirds — to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until frosty.
Strain into a chilled shot glass.
For a full-size cocktail, double everything to 1 oz each and strain into a chilled coupe.
Drink in one clean motion.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on the rim

name: Lemon Drop
description: Vodka-lemonade compressed into candy form, with a sugared rim as the wrapper. Puckers first, forgives quickly.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s at Henry Africa's in San Francisco, widely described as America's first "fern bar."

steps: Rub a lemon wedge around the rim of a shot glass, then dip the rim in sugar to coat it.
Add the vodka, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until well chilled.
Strain carefully into the sugar-rimmed shot glass without disturbing the rim.
Shoot it, then bite the lemon wedge if you kept one on the side.
recipe.garnish: Sugared rim and a small lemon wedge

name: Mind Eraser
description: A stratified vodka-and-coffee contraption drained through a straw from the bottom up. Does exactly what the label promises.
funFact: House rules require draining it in one continuous pull from the bottom — coffee liqueur first, fizzy water last — making it a carbonated Black Russian in a hurry.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice cubes.
Pour the coffee liqueur first so it settles at the bottom.
Gently pour the vodka over the ice as the middle layer — do not stir.
Slowly top with chilled soda water to form the fizzy top layer.
Drop in a straw that reaches the bottom and drink in one continuous pull, from coffee liqueur up through the soda.
recipe.garnish: None (served with a straw)

name: Pickleback
description: A whiskey shot immediately chased by cold pickle brine, which erases the burn like it never happened. Chemistry-adjacent magic in two small glasses.
funFact: Bartender Reggie Cunningham poured the first one at Brooklyn's Bushwick Country Club in 2006, using brine from a jar of McClure's pickles stored at the bar.

steps: Chill the pickle brine in the fridge ahead of time — cold brine is essential.
Pour the whiskey into one shot glass and the brine into a second, matching shot glass.
Shoot the whiskey first, in one go.
Immediately chase it with the full shot of pickle brine and let it wipe out the burn.
recipe.garnish: None (a small dill pickle spear on the side is a nice touch)

name: Vegas Bomb
description: A whisky-peach-cranberry payload dropped into an energy drink. Detonates on contact with bachelor parties.
glassware: Shot glass dropped in a pint glass
funFact: Skip the energy-drink plunge and the shot inside goes by its own poker-table name: the Royal Flush.

steps: Stir or briefly shake the whisky, peach schnapps, and cranberry juice with ice, then strain into a shot glass.
Pour the energy drink into a sturdy pint glass, filling it about a third of the way.
Drop the full shot glass straight into the energy drink.
Drink immediately in one continuous go.
Skip the drop and sip the strained shot on its own and you have a Royal Flush.
recipe.garnish: None

name: Washington Apple
description: An orchard compressed into a shot glass: whisky, sour apple, and cranberry doing a crisp autumn impression all year round.
funFact: It salutes Washington State, grower of most of America's apples — yet its traditional whisky is Canadian.

steps: Add the whisky, sour apple schnapps, and cranberry juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled shot glass.
For a full cocktail, use 1 oz of each ingredient and strain into a chilled coupe over the same spec.
Garnish and drink while ice cold.
recipe.garnish: Thin green apple slice on the rim (optional for the shot)

name: Amaretto Sour
description: Almond liqueur brightened with lemon into something between marzipan and lemonade. Long dismissed as a starter drink, lately rebuilt with respect.
funFact: Bartender Jeffrey Morgenthaler famously declared in 2012 that he makes the world's best Amaretto Sour by adding cask-proof bourbon and egg white — a spec many bars now follow.

ingredients.amount: 0.5 oz / 15 ml (about half an egg white)

steps: Add the amaretto, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup, and egg white (if using) to a shaker with no ice and dry shake hard for 10 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake again for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Strain over fresh ice into a rocks glass.
Let the foam settle for a moment, then garnish.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel and a brandied cherry

name: Aviation
description: Gin, maraschino, lemon, and a whisper of crème de violette tinting the glass the pale gray-blue of a cloudy sky. Delicate, floral, and easy to overdo.
funFact: Crème de violette vanished from the American market for decades, so generations of bartenders made colorless Aviations until imports resumed in 2007.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Combine the gin, maraschino, crème de violette, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until frost forms on the tin.
Double strain into the chilled coupe so no ice shards cloud the pale sky-blue color.
Keep the violette light — more than a bathtub-gin whisper turns it soapy.
recipe.garnish: Brandied cherry dropped to the bottom of the glass

name: Bee's Knees
description: Gin, honey, and lemon — a Prohibition-era formula in which the honey did double duty as flavor and camouflage. Named with era-appropriate slang for 'the best.'
funFact: During Prohibition, honey and lemon conveniently masked the harsh bite of bathtub gin; one popular attribution credits Frank Meier of the Ritz Paris with the recipe.

ingredients.item: Honey syrup (3:1 honey to warm water)

steps: Make honey syrup by stirring 3 parts honey into 1 part warm water until fully dissolved; let cool.
Chill a coupe.
Add gin, honey syrup, and fresh lemon juice to a shaker with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist

name: Blood and Sand
description: Scotch, cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth, and orange juice in improbable equal-parts harmony — one of the only classics brave enough to mix Scotch with juice.
funFact: It was named after the 1922 Rudolph Valentino bullfighting film 'Blood and Sand' and preserved for posterity in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the Scotch, cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth, and fresh orange juice to a shaker with ice — equal parts, per the classic 1930 Savoy spec.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist, expressed over the top, plus an optional cherry

name: Brandy Crusta
description: Cognac, curaçao, maraschino, and lemon dressed in a full sugared crust and an extravagant ribbon of lemon peel. The peacock ancestor of the Sidecar.
funFact: Joseph Santini's 1850s New Orleans creation is credited with introducing elaborate citrus garnish to the cocktail — the entire glass rim is 'crusted' in sugar.

ingredients.amount: About 2 tbsp on a small plate

steps: Prepare the glass: rub a lemon wedge around the outside of the rim of a small wine glass, then roll the rim in superfine sugar to form a wide, even crust. Chill the glass.
Cut a long, wide ribbon of lemon peel in one continuous spiral and coil it inside the glass so it lines the rim.
Add the cognac, curaçao, maraschino, lemon juice, and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain carefully into the prepared glass without disturbing the sugar crust.
recipe.garnish: The sugared rim and a long spiral of lemon peel coiled inside the glass

name: Caipirinha
description: Cachaça muddled with whole lime and sugar in the glass it is served in. Brazil's national cocktail: rustic by design, lethal by volume.
funFact: One popular legend traces it to a São Paulo folk remedy for the Spanish flu made with lime, garlic, and honey — over time the garlic left and the cachaça stayed.

ingredients.amount: Half a lime, cut into 4 wedges
Cracked or cubed, to fill the glass

steps: Add the lime wedges and sugar directly to a sturdy rocks glass.
Muddle firmly to press out the juice and lime oils and dissolve the sugar — press, don't pulverize the pith.
Fill the glass with cracked ice and pour in the cachaça.
Churn with a spoon (or cap and give one short shake back into the glass) until the outside frosts.
Serve in the same glass with a short straw.
recipe.garnish: The muddled lime wedges in the glass; add a fresh lime wheel if you like

name: Clover Club
description: Gin, raspberry, lemon, and egg white shaken into a rosy cloud. Pretty in pink but pre-Prohibition to the bone.
funFact: It was named for a Philadelphia club of lawyers, writers, and industrialists who met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel from the 1880s onward — hardly the crowd its color suggests.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add gin, raspberry syrup, fresh lemon juice, and egg white to a shaker with no ice and dry shake hard for 10-15 seconds to whip the foam.
Add ice and shake again for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe and let the rosy foam cap settle before garnishing.
recipe.garnish: Three raspberries on a pick, laid across the foam

name: Corpse Reviver No. 2
description: Gin, Cointreau, Lillet, and lemon over an absinthe rinse — a member of the Victorian family of hangover 'cures' and comfortably the best of them.
funFact: Harry Craddock's 1930 'Savoy Cocktail Book' warns that 'four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again.'

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe: add the absinthe, swirl to coat the inside, and dump (or spray the glass with an atomizer).
Add the gin, Cointreau, Lillet Blanc, and fresh lemon juice to a shaker with ice — equal parts.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Heed the Savoy's warning: stop before the fourth.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist or a cocktail cherry

name: Cosmopolitan
description: A blush-pink shard of the 1990s: citrus vodka, cranberry, lime, and orange liqueur served up with maximum poise. Dismissed as a fad, it simply never left.
funFact: Its origin is disputed among several American bartenders, but nobody disputes what made it a global icon: Carrie Bradshaw ordering round after round on 'Sex and the City.'

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer.
Add the citrus vodka, Cointreau, cranberry juice, and fresh lime juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds — you want it ice cold with a slight frothy blush.
Double strain into the chilled martini glass.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist — flame it over the surface for the full 90s effect

name: Daiquiri
description: Rum, lime, and sugar shaken to a snowy chill — nothing more is needed and nothing less will do. Often mistaken for its frozen, blended descendants.
funFact: It takes its name from Daiquirí, a beach and village near Santiago de Cuba, where American mining engineer Jennings Cox is credited with mixing it around 1898.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Add the rum, fresh lime juice, and simple syrup to a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake very hard for 12-15 seconds — the Daiquiri wants real dilution and a snowy chill.
Double strain into the chilled coupe so it pours crystal clear with a fine frost.
recipe.garnish: Thin lime wheel on the rim

name: Gimlet
description: Gin and lime cordial, sharp and to the point — named, fittingly, after a small boring tool. A naval ration that retired ashore and never left.
funFact: Rose's lime cordial, patented in 1867, preserved lime juice without alcohol for the Royal Navy — the same lime rations that earned British sailors the nickname 'limeys.'

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the gin and lime cordial to a mixing glass filled with ice.
Stir for 20-30 seconds until thoroughly chilled and slightly diluted — with cordial (no fresh juice) the drink stays silky when stirred.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Prefer it brighter? Swap in a shake and adjust cordial to taste — the naval classic is simply gin and cordial, sharp and to the point.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel or lime twist

name: Hemingway Daiquiri
description: A bone-dry daiquiri sharpened with grapefruit and maraschino, built to a novelist's exacting and immodest specifications. Also answers to 'Papa Doble.'
funFact: Ernest Hemingway, wary of sugar, asked Havana's El Floridita for his daiquiri with no sugar and double rum — the resulting 'Papa Doble' was named in his honor.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the rum, fresh grapefruit juice, maraschino, and fresh lime juice to a shaker with ice — no sugar, as Papa demanded.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
Expect it bone-dry and bracing; add a bar spoon of simple syrup only if it's too austere for your taste.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel

name: Jack Rose
description: Applejack, grenadine, and citrus in a blushing pre-Prohibition sour. Orchard fruit with a literary pedigree and a slightly shady name.
funFact: Jake Barnes drinks a Jack Rose in a Paris hotel bar in Ernest Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises' (1926).

ingredients.item: Applejack (bonded if you can find it)

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the applejack, fresh lemon (or lime) juice, and grenadine to a shaker with ice — use a proper pomegranate grenadine, not neon syrup.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
recipe.garnish: Thin apple slice or a lemon twist

name: Last Word
